interviewQuestions.question: What is write amplification, and why does it matter for both SSD performance and lifespan?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
⭐ **Q: What is write amplification, and why does it matter for both SSD performance and lifespan?**

I'd define it as the ratio of physical writes the SSD actually performs internally to the logical writes the host requested. It exists because flash can't overwrite in place: a logical overwrite gets redirected to a fresh page, the old page is marked stale, and garbage collection later relocates any still-live neighbors before erasing that block — all of that relocation counts as extra physical writes the host never asked for.

The performance angle: under sustained random writes, the SSD may be doing several times more physical I/O than the host thinks it's issuing, which shows up as degraded sustained write throughput compared to burst performance. The lifespan angle: every physical write consumes one of a flash cell's finite erase cycles, so a write amplification factor of 5 effectively divides the drive's usable lifetime by 5 for that workload.

Concretely, this is why enterprise SSDs are often shipped with significant **over-provisioning** — extra spare flash the host never sees — specifically to give the garbage collector more room to work with and keep write amplification low.

**Testing:** whether you understand write amplification as a consequence of the erase-before-write constraint, and can connect it to real operational decisions like over-provisioning.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Write amplification, cause and consequence

interviewQuestions.question: Why does an SSD need both garbage collection and wear leveling — aren't they solving the same problem?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
**Q: Why does an SSD need both garbage collection and wear leveling — aren't they solving the same problem?**

I'd separate the two by the problem each actually solves. Garbage collection reclaims **space**: it finds blocks with a mix of live and stale pages, relocates the live pages elsewhere, and erases the block so it can be reused — without this, the SSD would eventually run out of writable space even though much of the data on it is logically deleted.

Wear leveling manages **durability**: since each cell only survives a finite number of erase cycles, wear leveling makes sure erases are spread evenly across all physical blocks, so no single 'hot' block wears out and fails long before the rest of the drive. Without it, a naive FTL that always reused the most convenient free blocks would create failure hotspots.

They do interact, though — garbage collection's relocation naturally moves data around, which wear leveling can use as an opportunity to also rebalance wear, sometimes even relocating cold, rarely-changed data purely to free up an over-worn block. So they're complementary: GC keeps space usable, wear leveling keeps that usable space alive for as long as possible.

**Testing:** whether you can distinguish two related-but-distinct FTL responsibilities instead of conflating them into one vague 'flash management' bucket.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Garbage collection vs wear leveling
